title: School website
text: The school logo is on every page. This helps parents know they are still on the school website. The menu uses short words, such as News and Contact. Parents can look for these words when they need help. They do not have to read every page first.

title: University website
text: A large photo shows students working together. New visitors may feel that they can meet people here. The Apply button is beside the photo. People can read about the university and then start their form. They do not need to look at the bottom of the page for this button.

title: Online learning website
text: After each answer, the website shows a green tick or a red cross. This tells learners if their answer is right. They can try again when it is wrong. A line shows how much work is left. Learners may want to keep going and finish the lesson.

title: Language learning website
text: The website shows one short lesson at a time. This may help new learners feel less worried about the work. A speaker button lets them hear each word again. They can listen before they speak. The pictures also help them understand words when they cannot read all the text.

title: Library website
text: A large search box is near the top of the page. People looking for a book can start here. They do not have to look through long lists first. The book pictures may help younger readers too. They can look for a cover they know when the title is hard to read.

title: Science website
text: Small headings break the long page into parts. Readers can stop after one part and come back later. A picture beside each part helps them understand the words. When a picture is far from its text, readers may look at the wrong one and find the information hard to follow.

title: Children's games website
text: The game buttons are large and far apart. Children can tap one without hitting the next button. Each game also has a different picture. Children who cannot read every title can use these pictures to choose. The Play button is always green, so they know what to look for next.

title: Charity website
text: A photo shows a family outside their new home. This helps visitors see what the charity does for people. A Give button sits beside the picture. Visitors may want to help after seeing the family. The words under the button tell them where their money will go.

title: Animal rescue website
text: Each animal has a name and a photo. Visitors may see the animals as pets they could know, not just names on a list. A button under each photo opens more information. People can learn about one animal before they ask to visit the rescue centre.

title: Environmental campaign website
text: The page shows the same beach before and after a clean. Visitors can see the change without reading much text. This may make them feel that helping can do something. A Join button below the pictures gives them a way to take part while they are thinking about the beach.

title: Volunteering website
text: Visitors can choose a day before they see the jobs. This helps them look for work they have time to do. The website does not ask them to read about every job first. A map also shows where each job is. People can choose somewhere near their home.

title: Council website
text: The menu uses words such as Bins, Roads and Homes. These words help people look for the thing they need. A menu with only pictures may be harder to understand. Some visitors may not know what the pictures mean, so they may open several pages before they find the right one.

title: Medical clinic website
text: The phone number is large and near the top. People who need to call can find it before reading about the clinic. The page also says when the clinic is open. This helps visitors decide what to do next. They may call now or choose another day for their visit.

title: Gym website
text: Photos show people of different ages in a class. A new visitor may feel that the gym has a place for them too. The page shows a short first class beside these photos. This may make joining feel less hard for someone who has never been to a gym before.

title: Sports club website
text: The next match is the first thing visitors see. Fans can find the day and time without reading older news. A button beside the date opens the ticket page. This helps people move from finding a match to buying a ticket. The club does not ask them to search again.

title: Photography website
text: One large photo fills the top of the page. Visitors can see the photographer's work before they read about it. This may help them decide if they like the pictures. A small Contact link may be harder to find, so some people may leave without asking about a photo session.

title: Design portfolio website
text: Each project has a picture and a short name. Visitors can choose a project by looking at the pictures first. This helps people who do not know the designer's work. The same Back button appears on every project page. Visitors can return to the gallery and look at another project.

title: Author website
text: A picture of the newest book is beside a short part of the story. Visitors can read this before they buy the book. They may want to know what happens next. A Read More button can keep them on the website while they learn about the writer and the story.

title: Home repair website
text: Photos show a broken door and the same door after a repair. Visitors can see the kind of work the person does. This may help them decide whether to call. The phone number is beside the photos, so they can ask for help while they are looking at the work.

title: Bank website
text: The website uses the same blue menu on every page. People can look in the same place for their account or for help. This may make them feel less lost. If the menu moves to a new place, visitors may spend more time looking for a link they used before.

title: Insurance website
text: A short list shows what each plan gives people. Visitors can look across the list and see differences. This may help them choose what they need. Small words at the bottom can be hard to read, so visitors may miss a rule about something the plan does not pay for.

title: Property website
text: Large photos let people look inside each home before they visit. A map helps them see where the home is. These two things answer different questions. Someone may like a room but need to check the area too. Keeping the map nearby helps them make that choice on the same page.

title: Job search website
text: The job page shows the pay and place near the title. People can check these details before they read the whole page. This may save them time when they need work near home. A Save button lets them keep a job and look at it again before they send a form.

title: Crowdfunding website
text: A line shows how much money a project has now. Visitors can see how far it is from its goal. They may want to help the project reach the end of the line. The page also shows who is asking for the money, so visitors can read about that person first.

title: Discussion forum
text: The newest answers appear under the first question. Readers can follow the talk from the start. A name beside each answer helps them see who is speaking. When several answers use the same colour, the names become more important. Without them, readers may think one person wrote all the answers.

title: Clothing shop
text: Visitors can choose their size before they browse the clothes. The website then hides items that are not available in that size. This saves visitors from opening several products they cannot buy. Showing the number of remaining items also explains why the page looks different after they make their choice.

title: Supermarket website
text: The search bar stays at the top while customers scroll through the food. People can add milk and then search for bread without returning to the homepage. A small basket total changes after each item is added. This response helps customers check that the website has received their choice.

title: Crafts marketplace
text: A photograph of the maker appears beside each product. This connects the object with a person and may make the shop feel more personal. However, the seller's message button is hidden inside a dropdown menu. Visitors with a question may leave because they cannot see how to contact the maker.

title: Second hand marketplace
text: Some product thumbnails are very dark, so visitors cannot see the condition of the items before opening them. They may spend time checking things they do not want. A larger picture would show more detail, but the page first asks visitors to decide using these small previews.

title: Technology website
text: The phone slowly turns when a visitor drags across its picture. This interaction lets people examine the back and sides as well as the screen. It may keep them looking at the product for longer. The price remains beside the picture, so exploring the phone does not hide its cost.

title: Restaurant website
text: The booking form asks for the date before asking for a name. Visitors can check whether a table is available before they give personal details. This can make the booking process feel shorter. A message beside the final button also tells them that the restaurant will send a confirmation email.

title: Bakery website
text: When a customer selects a cake size, both the picture and the price change. This helps them connect a larger cake with its extra cost. If only the photograph changed, customers might not notice the price difference. Showing both changes together gives them more information before they add the cake.

title: Food delivery website
text: A visitor enters an address before the website shows restaurants. This stops them choosing food from somewhere that cannot deliver to them. However, a long form at this early stage may feel like too much work. Someone who only wants to browse may close the page instead of continuing.

title: Hotel website
text: Room photographs appear above the booking buttons, while extra charges are shown much further down. Visitors may choose a room before they notice the full price. When the final total is higher, they may feel surprised. Keeping the charges near the first price would help people compare rooms earlier.

title: Campsite website
text: The map uses tent icons to show the camping areas. Visitors can see which places are close to the lake or the toilets. Labels beside the icons help people understand the symbols. Without these words, someone visiting the campsite for the first time may choose an area for the wrong reason.

title: Airline website
text: Each stage of the booking has a number and a name. Passengers can see whether they are choosing flights, seats or luggage. This helps them understand what comes next. The page also keeps their travel dates visible, so they can check the booking while moving through the different forms.

title: Journey planner
text: The website asks visitors to choose from a list after they begin typing a station name. This can help them avoid spelling mistakes. It also shows places with similar names. Visitors still need to read the full label, because choosing the first result may send them to a different station.

title: Tourist guide
text: A map appears beside the list of places to visit. When visitors select a place, its point on the map changes colour. This connects the name with its position in the town. People planning a day out can see which places are close together before deciding where to go.

title: Museum website
text: A short opening times section appears before the museum's history. Families planning a visit can find the information they need first. The ticket button uses the same blue colour on every page. Once visitors know this colour, they can look for it when they are ready to book.

title: Art gallery website
text: The large spaces around the paintings keep other pictures away from them. Visitors can look at one work without several nearby images taking their attention. However, the artist's name appears only when a pointer moves over the painting. People using a phone may not discover the name before opening it.

title: Cinema website
text: The seat map changes a chosen seat from blue to yellow and adds its number to a list. Visitors can check their choice in two ways. This is helpful when nearby seats look similar. A Remove link beside each number also lets them change their mind without starting the whole booking again.

title: Theatre website
text: A short video starts playing as soon as the homepage opens. It may catch attention, but its music can interrupt visitors who only want show times. The Stop button is small and has no label. Some people may close the website because they cannot quickly find a way to stop the sound.

title: Festival website
text: The programme can be viewed by day or by stage. These tabs help visitors plan in different ways. Someone following one singer can check the stage, while a person with a Saturday ticket can choose that day. Keeping both views on one page means visitors do not need to search again.

title: Musician website
text: The website lets fans play a short part of each song before opening the shop. New listeners can hear the music before deciding to buy it. The Play button changes to Pause while a song is running. This tells visitors both what is happening and how to stop it.

title: Video game website
text: The first button says Watch the Game rather than simply More. Visitors can understand that it opens a video before selecting it. This may make them more willing to try the button. The video also has a visible close icon, so they can return to the page when they finish watching.

title: News website
text: Large headlines help readers notice the main stories, but several moving adverts sit between them. These adverts can pull attention away while people are reading. Some visitors may lose their place when they return to the story. A page with fewer moving parts may be easier for those readers to follow.

title: Online magazine
text: The magazine shows three related stories after each article. Visitors who enjoyed the first piece have somewhere else to go without returning to the menu. However, the pictures are larger than the article's final paragraph. Readers may move to another story before noticing that the first one has not finished.

title: Travel blog
text: The writer puts captions below photographs of stations and streets. These words help visitors connect a picture with a real place. A link in each caption opens a map. Readers planning the same journey can check where a photograph was taken instead of searching for the location themselves.

title: Recipe website
text: The recipe has checkboxes beside the ingredients. Cooks can mark what they have already added and then return after looking away from the screen. This can help them avoid adding something twice. A button clears the boxes, so the same recipe can be used again on another day.

title: Film review website
text: The review score appears beside the title, but the explanation is lower on the page. Visitors can make a quick choice using the score alone. Some may leave without reading why the reviewer gave it. This gives the number more power than the longer discussion of the film's strengths and problems.

title: Clothing shop
text: The clothing shop uses the same colour palette on its website and packaging, which strengthens its branding. Customers who arrive from a social media advert can recognise the shop immediately. However, the sale banner uses a brighter colour than the product photographs. This gives discounts greater visual importance and may encourage visitors to browse offers before new collections.

title: Crafts marketplace
text: Photographs of tools and unfinished objects appear beside the finished products. These images show the making process, giving visitors a reason to connect the prices with time and skill. The handwritten headings support this personal tone, although the smaller handwritten descriptions may take longer to read when customers are comparing several similar items.

title: Technology website
text: The homepage hero places a brightly lit laptop against an almost black background. This contrast makes the product the main point of attention before visitors reach its specifications. Because the first call to action says Explore rather than Buy, the journey begins with discovery. Visitors are encouraged to examine the product before considering its price.

title: Bakery website
text: A photograph of a baker carries more visual weight than the delivery information below it. Visitors may first connect the business with personal care and handmade food. Yet customers ordering a birthday cake need dates as well as atmosphere. If those details remain outside the first screen, the emotional appeal may delay a practical decision.

title: Hotel website
text: The room cards follow the same grid, with photographs, prices and buttons in matching positions. This consistency helps guests compare equivalent details without learning a new layout for each room. A larger card for the premium suite breaks that pattern. It may attract more attention even when a cheaper room would meet the visitor's needs.

title: Airline website
text: The cheapest fare is printed in large type, while luggage charges appear in smaller text underneath. This visual hierarchy can make the first price feel more important than the final cost. Travellers comparing airlines may remember the larger number and only discover the extra charges after they have already spent time entering their details.

title: Tourist guide
text: The guide uses a consistent blue line to connect photographs with points on a map. Visitors can link an attractive location to a place they could actually visit. This supports planning as well as browsing. On a phone, the map moves beneath the photographs, so visitors must scroll between the two kinds of information.

title: Art gallery website
text: Wide areas of whitespace separate the artworks, giving each image the attention usually associated with a physical gallery. The restrained layout may encourage visitors to examine individual pieces slowly. However, the Next button is much smaller than the paintings. People who do not recognise this navigation convention may miss the rest of the collection.

title: Theatre website
text: Serif headings and photographs of the old auditorium connect the theatre with its history. This visual identity may appeal to visitors looking for an established cultural venue. The booking form uses plain sans-serif text and short instructions, changing the tone when practical details matter. Visitors can therefore move from the theatre's story to a more direct task.

title: Musician website
text: Album covers form the main navigation, so existing fans can choose music they recognise without reading a menu. New listeners may have less confidence because the covers do not explain the differences between albums. Adding visible titles gives them another route into the collection while keeping the visual focus on the musician's work.

title: News website
text: The largest headline sits above several smaller stories, creating a clear order of importance. Readers may treat that first story as the day's main event because it receives the most space. This is an editorial effect as well as a layout choice: visitors encounter the newspaper's priorities before choosing which subject interests them personally.

title: Travel blog
text: The writer places practical maps between personal photographs and stories. This arrangement allows readers to enjoy the journey while also collecting information for their own trip. However, links to hotel bookings look exactly like links to earlier posts. Visitors may leave the blog unexpectedly because the design does not distinguish between these different destinations.

title: Film review website
text: A large star rating gives visitors an immediate judgement, while the detailed review appears below. This suits readers making a quick viewing choice but may reduce attention to the writer's argument. When the score remains visible as visitors scroll, it can continue to shape their expectations even while they read more balanced comments.

title: University website
text: The navigation groups courses by subject rather than by department name. Applicants can begin with an interest they understand instead of needing to know the university's internal structure. This supports visitors who are new to higher education. The course pages then repeat the same headings, helping applicants compare entry requirements, teaching and costs across different subjects.

title: Language learning website
text: The lesson menu shows completed topics in colour and leaves future topics grey. This gives learners a visible record of progress and a reason to return. However, grey buttons can also look unavailable. If learners are allowed to choose any topic, the visual convention may make the course seem more restricted than it really is.

title: Science website
text: The diagrams use numbered labels that match the paragraphs beside them. Readers can connect a technical explanation with the correct part of the image. This may help learners follow a process without holding every detail in memory. When the numbers are missing from the phone version, that connection becomes harder to maintain.

title: Charity website
text: The donation button is the only orange element on a mostly white page. Its contrast draws attention after visitors read the project story, giving them an immediate way to respond. The button's label names a specific action, such as Provide a Meal. This connects the payment with a result rather than presenting it as an unexplained transaction.

title: Environmental campaign website
text: A slider lets visitors compare two photographs of the same forest. Moving it reveals the difference gradually, asking people to take part in the comparison. This interaction may hold attention longer than two separate pictures. The dates beneath the images are important because they show the period of change and limit what visitors can reasonably conclude.

title: Council website
text: The homepage gives equal space to every council service, which makes the grid look regular but hides differences in demand. Someone reporting a missed collection must scan the same number of choices as someone researching a rare licence. A consistent layout can therefore appear orderly while still requiring considerable searching from its most frequent visitors.

title: Gym website
text: The homepage shows people beginning exercises rather than only experienced athletes lifting heavy weights. This choice can make the target audience seem broader and reduce the feeling that visitors must already be fit. A nearby beginner timetable turns that impression into a practical route, allowing interested visitors to find a class that matches the message.

title: Photography portfolio
text: The photographer removes prices from the portfolio pages and gives most of the space to images. Visitors are encouraged to judge the style before thinking about cost. This may suit clients seeking a particular visual approach, but those with a fixed budget must contact the photographer before knowing whether the service is possible for them.

title: Author website
text: The website repeats a small illustration from the book cover in its menus and section headings. This consistency creates a visual identity across the author's work. Readers arriving from a bookshop may recognise the illustration before reading the name. The website can then use that familiarity to introduce an unfamiliar title beside the existing books.

title: Bank website
text: The bank's pages use a formal tone, short headings and generous space around account information. Together, these choices can suggest an organised service rather than a busy advertising page. Yet this impression depends on the content too. If important fees are hidden behind several links, visitors may question the calm appearance once they discover the missing details.

title: Property website
text: The responsive design changes a three-column property grid into a single list on phones. Larger cards allow visitors to inspect photographs without zooming, but fewer homes are visible at once. People comparing many properties may need to scroll further. A saved list becomes more useful on the smaller screen because it keeps earlier choices within reach.

title: Crowdfunding website
text: The project page puts the funding total above the creator's explanation. Visitors see evidence of other people's support before learning how the project works. This may make the idea appear popular and worth exploring. It does not establish whether the plan is realistic, so the position of the budget details still matters to an informed decision.

title: Supermarket website
text: Although the basket updates immediately, the Add button gives no feedback after selection. Customers watching the product rather than the distant basket may assume nothing happened and tap again. The resulting duplicate items are a consequence of the interaction's limited visibility, illustrating how a technically completed action can still produce an uncertain user experience.

title: Second hand marketplace
text: The seller cards combine review scores with photographs, but the score occupies the brightest part of each card. Buyers may use this visible figure as a shortcut when judging trustworthiness, overlooking how few reviews support it. A five-star score based on one sale can therefore attract more attention than a slightly lower score supported by years of transactions.

title: Restaurant website
text: Displaying available tables before requesting personal details reduces the work visitors must invest before discovering whether a booking is possible. This sequence supports usability because each stage answers the question raised by the previous one. If the selected time disappears after login, however, that logical progression breaks and guests must repeat a decision they believed was complete.

title: Food delivery website
text: The interface gives paid restaurant placements larger photographs than ordinary results, while the sponsorship label remains faint. Hungry visitors scanning quickly may interpret prominence as evidence of relevance rather than payment. The visual arrangement consequently influences which businesses receive attention before customers have compared distance, delivery costs or the food itself.

title: Campsite website
text: The illustrated map creates a sense of the campsite's landscape, but its unlabelled symbols require visitors to interpret the designer's visual language. A leaf could indicate shade, woodland or an environmental restriction. Where these meanings remain uncertain, the attractive image increases the effort of choosing a pitch rather than directly supporting the booking task.

title: Journey planner
text: Colour distinguishes bus and rail routes, while written labels repeat the same information. This combination supports accessibility because visitors do not have to rely on colour alone. It also helps travellers checking a screenshot on a dim screen. Removing the labels in the mobile layout would weaken both benefits at the point where many travellers need them.

title: Museum website
text: A keyboard user can reach the ticket button, but the page provides no visible indication of which control currently has focus. The action remains possible, yet its position is uncertain. Visitors may press Enter on the wrong link or abandon the booking, showing why accessibility depends on visible interaction states as well as the existence of operable controls.

title: Cinema website
text: The seat map uses both colour and a written summary to confirm selections, giving visitors a way to check a dense visual interface. However, the summary updates below the visible screen on phones. Someone selecting several seats may miss that feedback and continue without noticing an unwanted choice, despite the same design working differently on a larger display.

title: Festival website
text: Artist portraits share an aspect ratio, so the programme forms a regular grid even though the original photographs differ. Visitors can scan the lineup without large images repeatedly interrupting its rhythm. Yet cropping every portrait identically removes instruments and performance settings, shifting attention from what artists do towards how their faces fit the festival's visual identity.

title: Video game website
text: The high-resolution background video demonstrates the game's visual detail, but its loading time delays the appearance of the Download button on slower connections. Visitors who already know the game must wait through material intended to introduce it. The opening therefore serves discovery and return visits unevenly, despite presenting the same interface to both audiences.

title: Online magazine
text: The magazine's narrow text column shortens each line, but a sticky sharing panel reduces it further on small screens. Readers encounter frequent line breaks that disrupt longer sentences. What appears to be a restrained desktop layout becomes a different reading experience on mobile, suggesting that readability cannot be judged from font size alone.

title: Recipe website
text: The cooking mode keeps the current instruction visible while hiding earlier stages. This can reduce distraction during a simple task, but it makes checking previous quantities more demanding. Cooks who need to move between stages may repeatedly leave the mode, so a feature designed around uninterrupted progress can be less useful during an ordinary, interrupted cooking process.

title: School website
text: News photographs dominate the homepage, while absence reporting sits inside a general information menu. The arrangement presents school life to prospective families but gives current parents a longer route to a frequent task. Its effectiveness therefore depends on whose visit is being considered: a persuasive introduction and a practical parent service require different priorities.

title: Online learning platform
text: The progress indicator counts completed pages rather than demonstrated understanding. Learners may feel encouraged by the rising total, yet they can advance without answering a question correctly. This feedback rewards movement through the interface more directly than mastery of the content, potentially shaping how students define success during a short practice session.

title: Library website
text: Alternative text identifies book covers by title and author, allowing people using screen-reading software to receive information that others obtain from the images. If the same details are immediately repeated in the adjacent link, however, each result becomes unnecessarily lengthy to hear. Accessibility improves when the relationship between image and surrounding content is considered together.

title: Children's games website
text: The rounded typeface contributes to a playful visual identity, but several similar letter shapes reduce legibility in the answer tiles. Children practising reading must distinguish the letters before solving the question. Here, the typography changes the difficulty of the learning task itself, so an entertaining appearance does not automatically support the site's educational purpose.

title: Animal rescue website
text: The gallery initially presents animals through appealing portraits, while care requirements appear after visitors open a profile. This encourages an emotional first response but can delay practical judgement. Someone may become attached to an animal before discovering that it needs a different home environment, creating tension between engagement with the photographs and a suitable adoption enquiry.

title: Volunteering website
text: Showing the duration beside every opportunity allows visitors to judge commitment before opening a description. This supports people who want to help but have limited time. When an application then requires unexpected training sessions, the earlier summary becomes misleading. The user journey needs to communicate the whole commitment, rather than only the length of the visible activity.

title: Medical clinic website
text: The appointment form highlights an error beside the relevant field and explains how to correct it. Visitors can respond without searching the entire form for a problem. A general warning at the top would provide less useful feedback, especially on a phone where the incorrect field might be several screen lengths away from the message.

title: Sports club website
text: The prototype gives supporters a direct route from the next fixture to its ticket options, but hides youth registration beneath several team pages. Testing only ticket purchases would therefore give a partial view of usability. Families joining the club face a different task, and their experience may reveal navigation problems that regular supporters never encounter.

title: Design portfolio
text: A subtle hover state reveals project titles only while the pointer rests on an image. This preserves an uncluttered gallery on desktop, yet visitors using touch do not encounter the same preview. If the title explains the project's purpose, hiding it changes what mobile visitors know before selecting work rather than merely changing the page's appearance.

title: Home repair website
text: Compressed project images appear sooner on a slow connection, helping visitors reach the quotation form without waiting for a large gallery. Excessive compression, however, can remove the surface detail that demonstrates the repairs. The appropriate balance depends on what the photograph needs to show, particularly when customers are examining workmanship rather than simply recognising a room.

title: Insurance website
text: The comparison table gives equal space to price and cover limits, inviting visitors to weigh both. On mobile, the cover columns move outside the viewport while the price stays visible. This responsive change alters the balance of the decision: the cheapest option becomes easier to compare than the restrictions that might explain its lower cost.

title: Job search website
text: Saving a vacancy produces a brief written message and changes the Save button to Saved. These two responses confirm the action without moving visitors away from their results. If the message disappears before someone reads it, the persistent button label still provides evidence, reducing the uncertainty that a short animation alone could leave behind.

title: Discussion forum
text: Replies are displayed according to popularity rather than time, so visitors encounter the most approved response before the earliest contribution. This may surface useful material, but it can also separate an answer from the question it addresses. Readers joining a complicated discussion must reconstruct its sequence while simultaneously judging the arguments within it.

title: Restaurant website
text: By organising its navigation around Visit, Eat and Book, the restaurant aligns its information architecture with visitors' intentions rather than its internal departments. The distinction matters most when users arrive with a specific task: locating dietary information requires a different route from reserving a table. If both routes end in the same undifferentiated menu, the apparent clarity of the labels does not survive the journey.

title: News website
text: The headline's visual salience establishes an editorial priority before readers have examined the evidence, particularly when its scale exceeds that of every competing story. This prominence can frame the event as urgent without explicitly describing it that way. A restrained colour palette does not neutralise the effect, because size and placement continue to direct attention even in the absence of bright colours.

title: Bank website
text: The application uses progressive disclosure to postpone less common questions until they become relevant, reducing the number of fields initially visible. That reduction can lower cognitive load, provided applicants still understand the full commitment. When a significant eligibility condition appears only after several completed stages, the same mechanism conceals a decision that users needed to make before investing their time.

title: Museum website
text: A highly legible ticket button remains difficult to use when keyboard navigation reaches it only after dozens of unrelated links. Visual prominence and navigational priority are therefore separate qualities. For visitors who cannot simply point at the button, the sequence of controls determines the practical user journey, exposing a limitation that a static screenshot of the homepage would not reveal.

title: Property website
text: The mobile-first layout preserves the photograph and monthly payment above the fold while moving fees into an expandable section. This allocation responds to the viewport's limited space, but it also establishes a hierarchy of financial information. Visitors can become interested in an apparently affordable home before encountering the charges that complicate that impression, making the layout consequential beyond its compact appearance.

title: Video game website
text: The download control resembles a decorative badge rather than a conventional button, weakening the visual affordance that might otherwise suggest an action. Existing fans may recognise it through prior experience, while newcomers must discover its function by trial. User testing limited to returning players could therefore overlook a barrier that is especially relevant to the campaign's stated aim of attracting a wider audience.

title: University website
text: Course titles appear as visually identical links, yet some open full descriptions while others launch application forms. This inconsistency forces applicants to predict destinations from institutional terminology rather than from the interface itself. A coherent user flow requires more than matching typography: visitors need enough information about the next action to move between exploration and commitment without accidentally crossing that boundary.

title: Crowdfunding website
text: The contribution button's brief animation confirms a successful selection, but the celebratory language appears before payment has been completed. This microinteraction may give supporters a premature sense of completion, obscuring the remaining step. The issue is not the animation alone; its meaning conflicts with the actual transaction state, so the feedback changes what users believe they have already accomplished.

title: Discussion forum
text: Ranking contributions by approval distributes visibility according to existing participation, allowing early responses to accumulate further attention. Newcomers may interpret their prominence as evidence of authority even when later posts provide stronger reasoning. Because the interface places endorsement ahead of chronology, it shapes the argument readers encounter, rather than simply presenting a conversation whose importance has been independently established.

title: Online learning platform
text: The interface offers hints only after an incorrect answer, making difficulty the gateway to additional support. This may preserve challenge for confident learners, but it assumes that everyone is willing to submit a guess. Students who interpret mistakes as failure may stop instead, so an identical sequence can produce different learning opportunities depending on the expectations visitors bring to it.

title: Charity website
text: The design brief prioritises completed donations, and the landing page accordingly gives its payment control greater prominence than its evidence links. This may increase conversion among visitors already convinced by the campaign, while leaving cautious readers searching for accountability. Evaluating only the number of payments would miss that difference between facilitating an existing intention and providing enough information to form one.

title: Airline website
text: The booking journey preserves selected flights when travellers return to earlier stages, reducing the risk that checking a condition will erase previous work. This continuity supports informed decisions rather than merely rapid progression. If the interface instead resets the journey, users face a practical penalty for investigating details, which can encourage commitment before uncertainty has actually been resolved.

title: Clothing shop
text: The product image changes immediately when a colour is selected, while the text label and stock message update beside it. These coordinated responses make the selection visible through more than colour alone. Their accessibility value depends on the complete interaction, however: a subtle image change offers limited confirmation if a keyboard user cannot determine which colour control currently has focus.

title: Language learning website
text: The lesson's contrast ratio may support legibility, yet the dense arrangement of instructions, timers and answer tiles still demands considerable attention. Accessibility cannot therefore be inferred from a single visual measurement. For learners processing unfamiliar vocabulary, the number of competing tasks contributes to cognitive load, potentially making interface management harder than the language question the activity intends to practise.

title: Library website
text: Search results expose format, availability and location before a title is opened, allowing readers to eliminate unsuitable editions early. This information architecture recognises that finding a book and obtaining it are related but distinct tasks. A catalogue that ranks relevance solely by title similarity may appear accurate while repeatedly directing visitors towards material they cannot borrow in the required form.

title: Food delivery website
text: The interface remembers a previous address without displaying it prominently, shortening the route to checkout for returning customers. That convenience depends on an assumption that their location has not changed. When users are ordering elsewhere, the hidden default can produce a confidently completed but incorrect order, demonstrating how reducing visible steps can also remove opportunities to question an inherited choice.

title: Design portfolio
text: Project metadata supplies roles, dates and clients beneath visually dramatic case studies, helping potential employers distinguish the designer's contribution from the team's wider work. If these details remain secondary to oversized claims of success, however, visitors must reconstruct responsibility themselves. The portfolio's persuasive authority then depends less on the images alone than on whether its supporting information makes professional authorship assessable.

title: Medical clinic website
text: The form retains entered details after identifying an error, allowing patients to correct one field without repeating sensitive information. This response reduces both practical effort and uncertainty about whether the request has been lost. A generic failure screen would interrupt the user journey at its most committed stage, when visitors have already invested time but have not yet secured an appointment.

title: Environmental campaign website
text: The comparison slider makes environmental change tangible through direct manipulation, but its persuasive force depends on photographs being meaningfully comparable. Different seasons or viewpoints could exaggerate the apparent contrast. Providing dates and image sources gives visitors a route to examine that construction, so the interaction supports scrutiny as well as the immediate emotional response produced by revealing the second image.

title: Festival website
text: At the responsive breakpoint, the timetable replaces simultaneous stage columns with separate tabs. This resolves a width constraint but removes the visual evidence of overlapping performances. Visitors can read each set more comfortably while finding conflicts harder to identify. The adaptation therefore changes the planning task itself, illustrating why mobile usability cannot be assessed solely by whether every desktop element remains available.

title: Insurance website
text: The comparison page labels its recommended plan with a prominent badge but provides the selection criteria through a faint secondary link. Visitors may attribute the recommendation to their own requirements without knowing whether commercial arrangements influence it. The resulting authority comes from presentation as much as explanation, particularly when the badge receives greater emphasis than the limits that distinguish the policies.

title: Job search website
text: The revised search interface retains applicants' filters across visits, an iteration that reduces repeated work for people following a stable set of requirements. Yet an unexplained retained filter can also narrow results invisibly when their circumstances change. Making the active constraints visible preserves the benefit of memory while allowing visitors to understand why apparently relevant vacancies have been excluded.

title: Recipe website
text: A high position in search results may bring readers directly to a recipe rather than its homepage, making the article their effective landing page. If navigation assumes prior familiarity with the site, these visitors begin without that context. Search engine optimisation can attract an audience, but the subsequent user journey determines whether they can locate quantities, instructions and related recipes once they arrive.

title: Animal rescue website
text: The enquiry form asks about household circumstances before revealing an animal's essential care requirements. Although this sequence collects useful information, it places the organisation's administrative needs ahead of the visitor's initial decision. Publishing those requirements earlier would let prospective adopters judge suitability before disclosing personal details, aligning the form's demands with the information necessary to justify completing it.

title: Volunteering website
text: The homepage represents every opportunity with an identical card, creating visual consistency while suppressing differences in commitment. A one-hour activity and a year-long role initially appear equivalent until their details are opened. Where duration is central to participation, the design's regularity can conceal the very distinction visitors need most, making an orderly overview less informative than its balanced appearance suggests.
